function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

Because they’re not in the same format, you can’t directly join or compare them without some kind of mapping or transformation. Here’s a quick checklist to help you get them aligned: | Step | What to do | Why it matters | |------|------------|----------------| | **1. Identify the source of each ID** | Confirm which system generates `culprit_unique_id` (e.g., your own database, an external API, etc.) and which system generates `crm_id`. | Knowing the origin helps you decide whether you can add a lookup table or if you need to call an API. | | **2. Check the format differences** | Are they numeric vs. alphanumeric? Do they have prefixes/suffixes? Is one a UUID while the other is a simple integer? | Understanding the exact difference lets you write a conversion rule. | | **3. Decide on a common key** | Either:
• Create a new “canonical” ID that both systems can reference.
• Use a lookup table that maps `culprit_unique_id` → `crm_id`. | A single key eliminates ambiguity when joining tables. | | **4. Build or update the mapping** | If you choose a lookup table:
• Add a column for the other system’s ID.
• Populate it via a script that queries both systems and matches records based on business logic (e.g., email, name, timestamp). | This table becomes your bridge between the two datasets. | | **5. Validate the mapping** | Run a few test joins to ensure that the mapped IDs actually refer to the same entity. | Prevents downstream errors in analytics or reporting. | | **6. Automate updates** | Set up a scheduled job that refreshes the mapping whenever new data arrives. | Keeps the bridge current without manual intervention. | ### Quick example (Python) ```python import pandas as pd # Load your internal data df_internal = pd.read_csv('internal.csv') # has culprit_unique_id # Load CRM data df_crm = pd.read_csv('crm.csv') # has crm_id # Suppose both share an email field that can be used for matching mapping = df_internal.merge(df_crm, on='email', how='inner')[['culprit_unique_id', 'crm_id']] # Save the mapping for future use mapping.to_csv('id_mapping.csv', index=False) ``` Once you have this mapping, you can join any future reports on the canonical key instead of trying to match raw IDs.
